frictionVectors.title: EU ENERGY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control through Sonatrach while expanding gas exports to Europe. European buyers seek diversification, limiting Algiers' long-term bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY FRONTIER
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali and Libya complicates Algeria's border security and regional diplomacy. External military and energy competition increasingly tests its non-intervention posture.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Angola remains heavily dependent on foreign-operated oil production and external capital despite efforts to strengthen national participation. Declining output and debt-service needs constrain sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: LOBITO CORRIDOR GEOPOLITICS
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European partners, and China are competing for influence around the Lobito rail corridor and neighboring copper-cobalt supply chains. Infrastructure financing could improve connectivity but deepen strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: NIGER TRADE DISRUPTION
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger and regional sanctions have exposed Benin's dependence on cross-border trade and the Cotonou corridor. External mediation and shifting border arrangements continue to affect port revenues.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Benin is strengthening maritime and northern border security with foreign training, equipment, and intelligence support. This improves resilience but increases reliance on external security partners.

frictionVectors.title: DIAMOND VALUE-CHAIN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured a stronger share of diamond marketing and benefits from its long-term partnership with De Beers, but remains exposed to weak global demand and foreign trading networks.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS DIVERSIFICATION
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to develop copper, nickel, and other critical minerals are attracting outside investors and infrastructure interests. The central challenge is converting new projects into domestic processing and fiscal gains.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD NATIONALIZATION
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is expanding state oversight of gold production and seeking greater control over licensing, refining, and exports. Insecurity, smuggling, and limited technical capacity constrain implementation.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Burkina Faso has reduced reliance on Western partners while deepening security ties with Russia and regional junta governments. The shift may increase autonomy from former partners but brings opaque financing and operational risks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals leverage
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking investment in nickel, rare-earth and other mineral projects, but limited state capacity leaves licensing and value capture vulnerable to foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border friction
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over accusations of rebel support and cross-border insecurity, complicating trade, transport and regional resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime-security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and other maritime assets attract European, Chinese and wider foreign interest, creating leverage over logistics and security infrastructure despite strong regulatory institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Undersea connectivity exposure
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's digital and communications infrastructure is strategically valuable but vulnerable to external ownership, cable disruptions and dependence on foreign financing.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure concentration
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail links and the Kribi deep-sea port are central to Cameroon's trade architecture, but financing, contractors and commodity corridors can limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and regional insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Separatist conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside instability near the Lake Chad basin, diverts state capacity and threatens transport routes, agricultural production and energy projects.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-resources model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel remain central to regime protection and counterinsurgency, while allegations of preferential access to gold and diamonds raise concerns over opaque resource concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Weak control over borders and transport corridors enables armed-group taxation, illicit mineral flows and dependence on foreign security and logistics providers.

highlights: External security ties are being recalibrated

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and political system remains heavily dependent on oil exports and the pipeline route through Cameroon, leaving sovereignty exposed to price shocks, infrastructure bottlenecks and foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Post-French security transition
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown of longstanding French military ties has increased uncertainty over external security guarantees as N'Djamena balances relations with Russia, regional governments and Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte Sovereignty Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with France over Mayotte remains a persistent sovereignty issue, intensified by migration controls and maritime enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited fiscal capacity leaves Comoros reliant on foreign aid, remittances, and external partners for infrastructure, energy, and maritime security.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in copper and cobalt processing, while Western governments seek alternative supply chains and stronger traceability.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Security
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east disrupts roads, mining zones, and border trade, with Rwanda, regional forces, and international actors shaping access and security outcomes.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state remains highly dependent on oil revenues and foreign operators, leaving public finances exposed to production and price shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and industrial projects provide strategic connectivity but reinforce concerns over debt exposure and limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Côte d’Ivoire is pursuing greater local processing and farmer income, but multinational buyers and volatile prices still constrain national control over the cocoa chain.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Concentration
frictionVectors.details: French, Gulf, Chinese, and other foreign investors remain important in ports, energy, and transport, creating growth while limiting strategic autonomy in key infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Presence
frictionVectors.details: US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and leverage but make Djibouti’s sovereignty dependent on competing external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: China-linked infrastructure and major port competition shape trade access and fiscal risk, while regional instability threatens the commercial value of Djibouti’s logistics network.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign financing and strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: Debt, IMF-linked reforms, and Gulf investment are expanding external influence over major infrastructure and land-development decisions. Cairo retains formal control but faces reduced policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains Egypt's central strategic concern, with disagreement over operating rules and drought management sustaining regional tension.

frictionVectors.title: Mature oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling production and limited diversification are increasing dependence on foreign operators, technical expertise, and external financing to sustain energy revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Malabo's infrastructure ambitions rely heavily on foreign contractors and state-backed lenders, creating leverage for outside partners despite strong domestic political control.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping routes attract competing regional and global security interests, increasing pressure on Asmara to align with external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide revenue but depend on foreign operators and technical capacity, creating persistent sovereignty risks despite state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics and market dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini remains deeply dependent on South African transport corridors, electricity systems, financial channels, and consumer markets, limiting independent infrastructure strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and manufacturing exposure
frictionVectors.details: Export industries rely on preferential access and multinational supply chains, leaving domestic resource control vulnerable to changes in regional trade rules and external demand.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and negotiations with international lenders constrain Addis Ababa's freedom over infrastructure, currency, and resource-sector policy while financing needs remain acute.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and maritime access disputes
frictionVectors.details: The GERD continues to drive tensions with Egypt and Sudan, while Ethiopia's pursuit of reliable Red Sea access creates friction with coastal states and regional powers.

frictionVectors.title: Post-coup contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in oil, manganese, and other extractive sectors. This improves bargaining leverage but risks investor uncertainty and slower project execution.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and port capacity remain critical to mineral revenues, leaving Gabon exposed to foreign operators, financing conditions, and infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing access and weak monitoring constrain Gambian control over marine resources. European and Asian fishing interests remain commercially important while provoking sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port modernization dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Banjul needs external capital and technical partnerships to improve regional transit capacity. Dependence on foreign financing can limit policy flexibility despite potential trade gains.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and gold governance
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and informal gold mining damages land and water while linking local networks to external equipment, finance, and smuggling channels. Government efforts to formalize the sector face entrenched interests and enforcement gaps.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked fiscal reforms narrow Accra's room to subsidize or rapidly expand strategic infrastructure. Ghana retains strong institutions, but external financing conditions influence resource and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is drawing major Chinese and other foreign capital into rail, port, and mining infrastructure. The state has increased leverage, but the scale of external financing and operators may leave Guinea dependent on outside supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Junta legitimacy and contracts
frictionVectors.details: Military rule has concentrated authority over mining licenses and infrastructure negotiations while delaying a credible democratic transition. Political uncertainty raises the risk of abrupt contract revisions, sanctions, and investor retaliation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and fisheries vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime enforcement enables foreign overfishing and reduces public capture of fisheries value. Bissau's port and logistics systems also require outside capital, increasing exposure to opaque concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Narco-trafficking and political capture
frictionVectors.details: Cocaine transit networks exploit weak institutions and threaten civilian control over security and customs agencies. External criminal finance can distort resource policy and undermine sovereignty more broadly.

highlights: Balancing China, Gulf capital, and Western lenders
Strategic ports and energy assets under scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is renegotiating its external financing exposure while seeking new investment in ports, rail, roads, and energy. Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders all retain leverage over major infrastructure choices.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu corridor remains strategically important for regional trade and resource exports, but security risks and local land concerns complicate development. Nairobi is also under pressure to secure greater domestic value from emerging mineral projects.

highlights: Water exports deepen dependence on South Africa

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa provide vital revenue but reinforce structural dependence on Pretoria. Delays, cost overruns, and security concerns around Phase II infrastructure continue to constrain Lesotho's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Mining Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's export base remains exposed to foreign apparel markets and externally owned diamond operations. Limited domestic processing leaves the country vulnerable to shifts in trade preferences and commodity prices.

highlights: Iron ore revival attracts major foreign operators
Port and concession governance remain decisive

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and potential offshore resources are being developed largely through foreign capital and concession frameworks. Liberia's fiscal gains remain dependent on contract enforcement, taxation, and local-content performance.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and neighboring states are competing for influence over ports, rail links, and mineral-export corridors. Weak infrastructure and limited state capacity reduce Monrovia's ability to capture downstream value.

highlights: Oil wealth remains split between rival power centers
Foreign patrons shape security and energy access

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed authorities continue to contest control over oil facilities, revenue flows, and appointments within the national energy system. Production remains vulnerable to blockades, factional bargaining, and disruptions to export terminals.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, Egypt, the UAE, and European states retain influence through military, political, and energy relationships. This external competition limits Libya's ability to establish unified control over strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Nickel, cobalt, and ilmenite draw sustained foreign capital
Resource governance outpaces local value capture

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed projects dominate nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral development. Madagascar remains exposed to disputes over royalties, environmental damage, land rights, and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Logging and Sovereignty Gaps
frictionVectors.details: Weak enforcement enables illicit timber extraction and informal mining in protected areas. International conservation and commodity networks provide resources but can also constrain national control over land-use decisions.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and creditor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Malawi's restructuring process and IMF program constrain fiscal and policy autonomy, with creditors and development partners exerting significant influence over public investment and subsidies.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel, power, and fertilizer dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity shortages and reliance on imported fuel and agricultural inputs leave the country exposed to exchange-rate shocks and external supply disruptions.

highlights: Junta asserts control over gold sector

frictionVectors.title: Gold sovereignty versus foreign operators
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pressing mining companies for higher state participation and revenue, but technical, financial, and security dependencies continue to limit autonomous control over gold production.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security and Russian dependence
frictionVectors.details: The breakdown of ties with France and Western partners has increased reliance on Russian security support while insurgency and territorial insecurity continue to disrupt transport and extractive activity.

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim governance
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas project with Senegal and international partners offers major revenue potential, but production timing, revenue-sharing, and local-content requirements remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and port concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports remain heavily tied to foreign capital, technology, and the Nouadhibou logistics corridor, limiting Mauritania's leverage over pricing and downstream value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos settlement and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago is advancing diplomatically, but the future of the UK-US military facility on Diego Garcia remains the core strategic constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Import-dependent energy system
frictionVectors.details: The island's dependence on imported fuel and limited domestic land and water resources exposes its infrastructure and economic model to shipping disruptions and external price shocks.

highlights: Western Sahara remains strategic fault line

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is using phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and infrastructure projects in the territory to reinforce its claim, drawing persistent legal and diplomatic opposition from Algeria and Polisario.

frictionVectors.title: External capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Gulf, and US investment supports ports, rail, automotive, and renewable projects, but competition among partners creates pressure to balance sovereignty with financing and technology access.

highlights: Ports and Gas Draw External Competition

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence continues to constrain state control around the Rovuma Basin and delays the full return of major LNG operations. Foreign military and private-security support remains important to protecting strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and Port Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms and Gulf-linked investors retain significant influence over LNG, logistics, and port development, limiting Mozambique's bargaining power despite large resource potential.

highlights: Oil and Green Hydrogen Raise Stakes

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of New Energy Assets
frictionVectors.details: International companies are moving quickly into offshore oil, uranium, green hydrogen, and critical minerals. Namibia is strengthening local-beneficiation and licensing rules, but capital and technical dependence remain substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Grid Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited water, transmission capacity, and port infrastructure could leave major projects dependent on foreign-built corridors and export agreements, weakening domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are seeking greater state control and revised terms in uranium and other extractive sectors, increasing confrontation with established foreign operators. Regulatory uncertainty and diplomatic rupture threaten production and revenue continuity.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency, border instability, and strained relations with regional institutions complicate access to trade corridors. Growing reliance on Russian security ties may reduce Western influence but creates a new external dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Production Losses
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, illegal refining, and weak enforcement continue to erode public control over petroleum revenues. International operators retain major technical and financial leverage despite regulatory reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Power Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: LNG expansion, pipelines, refineries, and electricity projects require substantial foreign capital and contractors. Chronic grid weakness and security risks limit Nigeria's ability to convert resource wealth into sovereign industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo remain a major source of diplomatic and sanctions risk. External scrutiny threatens access to premium supply chains and development finance.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Dependence on External Partners
frictionVectors.details: The government has improved formal mineral processing and traceability, but technology, finance, and security cooperation remain heavily shaped by foreign partners. This supports state capacity while narrowing autonomous policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore exploration uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe continues to court foreign partners for offshore hydrocarbons, but uncertain commercial reserves and limited state capacity constrain bargaining power and near-term revenue.

frictionVectors.title: External finance dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and budget support remain dependent on foreign donors and lenders, increasing exposure to competing Portuguese, Chinese, and multilateral priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater domestic capture from offshore oil and gas projects, creating tension with international operators and lenders while production revenues remain essential.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing access and maritime control
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing access, especially involving foreign fleets, remains politically sensitive as Senegal seeks stronger protection of coastal livelihoods and enforcement of its maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security footprint
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles must balance Indian, Chinese, European, and other maritime interests while preserving control over port access, surveillance infrastructure, and its extensive exclusive economic zone.

frictionVectors.title: Climate and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rising climate costs and dependence on tourism and external finance limit the state's room to develop fisheries and blue-economy assets without accepting outside capital and policy conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral dependency
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains dominated by foreign capital and export infrastructure, leaving the state vulnerable to commodity cycles and disputes over royalties, local processing, and environmental costs.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Freetown's port and transport corridors attract competing external investors, while the government seeks infrastructure upgrades without surrendering excessive strategic or fiscal control.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopia maritime access dispute
frictionVectors.details: Somalia's opposition to Ethiopia's attempted access arrangement in Somaliland reflects a direct sovereignty contest over ports and coastline, with regional mediation still required to prevent escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented control of offshore resources
frictionVectors.details: Foreign security partners, competing regional actors, and international energy companies are shaping access to Somalia's waters while federal and regional authorities struggle to establish unified control over fisheries and prospective hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS AND RAIL BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Chronic capacity and governance problems at Transnet constrain mineral exports and weaken South Africa's bargaining power with global commodity buyers. Private-sector participation may improve performance but risks foreign influence over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European states, and China are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and other minerals. Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation while managing investment dependence and geopolitical pressure.

frictionVectors.title: OIL-EXPORT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's fiscal system remains dependent on oil moving through Sudanese infrastructure, leaving revenue and exports exposed to conflict, sabotage, and external transit leverage. Chinese-linked operators remain important across the petroleum chain.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Juba relies heavily on neighboring states and international partners for mediation, security support, and humanitarian access. Elite competition and weak institutions continue to limit sovereign control over land, oil, and border corridors.

highlights: Gold and ports draw external competition

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival armed networks, while foreign buyers and regional intermediaries capture value outside effective state oversight. The conflict has transformed mineral access into a major channel of external influence.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA PORT PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and associated maritime infrastructure is strategically important to Gulf, Russian, Turkish, and other external actors. War-related dependence increases the risk that critical port and logistics decisions will be traded for political or military support.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The Dar es Salaam corridor is attracting Gulf, Chinese, Indian, and Western investment as partners compete for access to inland African markets and minerals. Tanzania is using this rivalry to expand infrastructure, but long-term control terms remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The government continues to demand greater domestic participation, tax capture, and processing from international mining firms. Disputes over licensing, local content, and environmental obligations could deter capital while strengthening bargaining leverage.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hinge

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a critical transshipment and landlocked-market gateway, but its expansion depends heavily on external finance, operators, and regional trade flows. This creates leverage for foreign commercial and political actors over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and political instability in Burkina Faso and northern Benin are increasing pressure on Togo's northern frontier. Expanded foreign security cooperation may improve resilience while narrowing independent control over border and transport policy.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia relies on European financial and trade channels while facing pressure to contain migration flows. This gives external partners significant leverage over domestic policy and border infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Gas import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and dependence on Algerian gas and imported energy expose Tunisia to supply and pricing risks. Fiscal pressure limits its ability to invest rapidly in alternatives.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline is central to Uganda's planned oil revenues but faces sustained environmental, financing, and reputational opposition. Uganda views the project as a sovereign development priority, while foreign lenders and campaigners challenge its terms and impacts.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed and other foreign-financed roads, power, and industrial projects support growth but increase exposure to external creditors and contractors. Debt-service constraints may narrow Kampala's room to renegotiate project conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using renewed interest in copper and cobalt to seek greater local processing, fiscal returns, and supply-chain influence. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, European, and North American investors creates leverage but also risks fragmented concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and transport bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Drought-related hydropower shortages and constrained regional transport infrastructure threaten mines and refining ambitions. Dependence on imported power and corridor access limits Zambia's ability to capture more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum leverage
frictionVectors.details: Harare is tightening controls on unprocessed mineral exports and seeking domestic beneficiation, but capital, technology, and market access remain heavily foreign-dependent. Chinese firms retain a strong position in lithium while Western and regional investors compete in other strategic minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and infrastructure fragility
frictionVectors.details: Unstable monetary conditions, electricity shortages, and rail constraints raise operating costs and weaken the state's negotiating position with mining companies. Resource revenues remain vulnerable to opaque contracting, rent capture, and external payment pressures.
